examples.title: Worked example: sort the tray (meet the player)
examples.objective: Learn the worked-example player controls (Step, Play, prediction checkpoints and the preset switcher) while sorting numbers into even/odd and prime/composite sets.

examples.title: Worked example: the shortest route across campus
examples.objective: Learn prediction checkpoints and answer-checking on the player while finding the shortest route through a small weighted graph, settling one vertex at a time.

examples.title: Worked example: building a power set by doubling
examples.objective: Build a power set by the include/exclude decision process, watching the subset count double at each element until it reaches 2^n.

examples.title: Worked example: building A × B on a grid
examples.objective: Build a Cartesian product A × B cell by cell on a grid and count the ordered pairs with the product rule |A × B| = |A| · |B|.

examples.title: Worked example: shading (A ∪ B) ∩ C′ on a Venn diagram
examples.objective: Compute a compound set expression one sub-expression at a time, tracking each partial result as a shading on a Venn diagram.

examples.title: Worked example: De Morgan’s law by a membership table
examples.objective: Prove a De Morgan law for concrete sets by building a membership table and showing that the two sides agree in every row.

variants.label: Variant: the other De Morgan law

examples.title: Worked example: a truth table, column by column
examples.objective: Build a truth table column by column, from the smallest sub-formulas outward, and classify the formula as a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency.

examples.title: Worked example: rewriting a negated conditional
examples.objective: Rewrite a negated formula by applying named equivalence laws one step at a time, then prove the rewrite by comparing truth-table columns.

examples.title: Worked example: is this argument valid?
examples.objective: Test an argument for validity by searching its truth table for a counterexample: a row where every premise is true and the conclusion is false.

examples.title: Worked example: quantifiers and negation on a small domain
examples.objective: Evaluate a quantified statement element by element over a finite domain, then form its negation by flipping the quantifier and check the negation on the same table.

examples.title: Worked example: the sum formula by induction
examples.objective: Prove a closed-form sum formula by mathematical induction, checking the base case and then the inductive step.

examples.title: Worked example: the square root of 2 is irrational
examples.objective: Prove a number is irrational by contradiction, using lowest terms and a parity argument to force a shared factor.

examples.title: Worked example: a direct proof, inference by inference
examples.objective: Prove a parity claim by direct proof, justifying each inference from the hypothesis to the conclusion.

examples.title: Worked example: a proof by contrapositive
examples.objective: Prove a statement by forming its contrapositive (negate both parts, then swap them) and proving that instead.

examples.title: Worked example: strong induction and prime factorization
examples.objective: Prove a claim by strong induction, using several earlier cases at once where ordinary induction offers only one.

examples.title: Worked example: transitive closure by Warshall’s algorithm
examples.objective: Compute the transitive closure of a relation with Warshall’s algorithm, allowing one intermediate vertex at a time.

examples.title: Worked example: equivalence classes mod 3
examples.objective: Show that a congruence relation is an equivalence relation and partition its set into the equivalence classes.

examples.title: Worked example: a property audit of one relation
examples.objective: Audit one concrete relation for reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity, reading each check in its matrix and its digraph at the same time.
examples.answer: reflexive, antisymmetric — neither an equivalence relation nor a partial order

variants.label: Variant: same-parity relation
variants.answer: reflexive, symmetric, transitive — an equivalence relation

examples.title: Worked example: from a partial order to its Hasse diagram
examples.objective: Build a Hasse diagram from a partial order by deleting reflexive loops and transitive edges, then placing the elements on levels.

examples.title: Worked example: binary search for 31
examples.objective: Trace binary search probe by probe on a sorted list, tracking lo, hi and mid until the target is found, and report the index together with the probe count.

examples.title: Worked example: insertion sort, pass by pass
examples.objective: Sort a list with insertion sort one pass at a time, growing a sorted prefix from the left and tracking the comparisons and shifts each inserted key costs.

examples.title: Worked example: counting a nested loop exactly
examples.objective: Count the exact number of inner-line executions of a triangular nested loop row by row, accumulate the running total, and check it against the closed form n(n + 1)/2.

variants.label: Variant: inner loop runs to n

examples.title: Worked example: a growth race at doubling inputs
examples.objective: Compare the growth families n, n log n and n squared by computing exact operation counts at doubling inputs, tracking each doubling factor, and naming the fastest-growing family.

examples.title: Worked example: Euclid’s algorithm for gcd(252, 198)
examples.objective: Use Euclid’s algorithm to find the gcd of two integers by repeated division, and justify the answer by dividing both original numbers by the result.

examples.title: Worked example: the inverse of 7 modulo 26
examples.objective: Find a modular inverse by running Euclid’s algorithm forward and back-substituting to a Bézout combination, and recognize the gcd test that decides whether an inverse exists at all.

examples.title: Worked example: 5^11 mod 13 by repeated squaring
examples.objective: Compute a modular power by repeated squaring: expand the exponent in binary, square the base step by step while reducing mod m, and multiply in only the powers selected by the 1-bits.

variants.label: Variant: exponent is a power of two

examples.title: Worked example: the sieve up to 30
examples.objective: Find all primes up to a stated bound with the sieve of Eratosthenes, crossing out multiples prime by prime starting at each prime squared, and check the surviving list by independent trial division.

examples.title: Worked example: ordered picks collapse into committees
examples.objective: Learn why combinations come from permutations by dividing out the r! orders of each group, watching every committee get overcounted the same number of times.

examples.title: Worked example: building Pascal’s triangle to find C(5, 2)
examples.objective: Learn to build Pascal’s triangle row by row using only the addition rule for neighboring entries, then read a binomial coefficient straight from the finished row.

examples.title: Worked example: a choice tree for the product and sum rules
examples.objective: Build a multi-stage choice as a tree level by level to apply the product rule, then add a disjoint alternatives group with the sum rule.

variants.label: Variant: a stage with one option

examples.title: Worked example: inclusion-exclusion on a Venn diagram
examples.objective: Count the union of two overlapping sets with inclusion-exclusion, tracking each region of the Venn diagram so the overlap is neither missed nor counted twice.

examples.title: Worked example: pigeonhole — how many socks guarantee a pair?
examples.objective: Use the pigeonhole principle by building the worst case placement by placement, so the guarantee is the first draw that has nowhere safe to go.

variants.label: Variant: guarantee three of a color

examples.title: Worked example: Tower of Hanoi in 7 moves
examples.objective: Learn how the recursive Tower of Hanoi strategy builds an optimal move sequence one subproblem at a time, and why n disks always take exactly 2^n − 1 moves.

examples.title: Worked example: iterating a recurrence to a closed form
examples.objective: Learn to solve a first-order recurrence by iterating it, spotting the pattern in a shifted column of terms, and proving the guessed closed form by induction.

examples.title: Worked example: a recursion tree with level costs
examples.objective: Expand a recursion tree level by level, compute the work per level and the leaf total, and add the level totals to solve a divide-and-conquer recurrence.

examples.title: Worked example: characteristic roots with initial conditions
examples.objective: Solve a two-term linear recurrence by forming and factoring its characteristic equation, applying the initial conditions to fix the constants, and checking the closed form against iterated terms.

examples.title: Worked example: Euler audit and building a circuit
examples.objective: Audit the degree parity of every vertex to decide whether an Euler trail exists, then trace a circuit edge by edge, marking each edge used exactly once.

examples.title: Worked example: adjacency list, degrees and a path
examples.objective: Build the adjacency list of a small graph from its picture, read every degree off the list, check the handshake sum, and use the list to settle a path question.

examples.title: Worked example: depth-first search with a stack
examples.objective: Run depth-first search with an explicit stack, showing every push and pop, the discovery order, the dead-end backtracks, and what happens to a stale stack entry.

examples.title: Worked example: coloring a graph, checking conflicts
examples.objective: Color a graph greedily in a stated vertex order, ruling colors out from neighbor conflicts at each step, and prove the number of colors used cannot be reduced.

variants.label: Variant: K4 needs a fourth color

examples.title: Worked example: breadth-first search order and layers
examples.objective: Run breadth-first search from a source vertex and read off the visit order and the layer (the fewest edges from the source) of every vertex it reaches.

examples.title: Worked example: Dijkstra shortest distances from A
examples.objective: Run Dijkstra's algorithm one settled vertex at a time, relaxing edges after each settle, to find the shortest distance from the source to every reachable vertex.

examples.title: Worked example: building a binary search tree by insertion
examples.objective: Build a binary search tree by inserting keys one at a time, following the smaller-left, larger-right rule at every node, and read the result with an inorder traversal.

examples.title: Worked example: building a Huffman code
examples.objective: Build a Huffman code by repeatedly merging the two lightest trees, then read each codeword off its root-to-leaf path and compute the expected code length.

examples.title: Worked example: searching a binary search tree
examples.objective: Search a binary search tree by following one root-to-leaf comparison path, once for a key that is present and once for a key whose absence is proved by an empty link.

examples.title: Worked example: three traversals of one tree
examples.objective: List one binary tree in preorder, inorder and postorder by applying each visiting rule recursively, and see how the same three rules act on a skewed tree.

examples.title: Worked example: a minimum spanning tree by Kruskal
examples.objective: Run Kruskal’s algorithm on a stated weighted graph, accepting or rejecting each link by the cycle test, until the accepted links form a minimum spanning tree.

variants.label: Variant: six stations, a tempting triangle

examples.title: Worked example: maximum flow by augmenting paths
examples.objective: Find a maximum flow by repeatedly pushing the bottleneck amount along an augmenting path, then certify the result with a cut of equal capacity.

variants.label: Variant: the trap — a backward step

examples.title: Worked example: a minimum cut from the residual network
examples.objective: Read a minimum cut off the final residual network: mark the vertices reachable from s, then add the capacities of the edges leaving that set.

variants.label: Variant: the cheap cut sits near s

examples.title: Worked example: auditing a flow, vertex by vertex
examples.objective: Verify a stated flow assignment by auditing both flow rules directly: capacity on every edge, then inflow against outflow at each intermediate vertex, summed from the edge list.

variants.label: Variant: one vertex does not balance

examples.title: Worked example: the augmenting path that has to cancel flow
examples.objective: Run Ford–Fulkerson with depth-first path choices on a network where greedy choices block the optimum, and explain the backward residual step — why canceling flow is legal and what the rerouting buys.

variants.label: Variant: a wider last link, no cancellation needed

examples.title: Worked example: minimizing with a Karnaugh map
examples.objective: Use a Karnaugh map to merge neighboring 1s into the largest possible groups and read off a minimal sum of products.

examples.title: Worked example: evaluating a ripple-carry adder
examples.objective: Evaluate a ripple-carry adder one column at a time from the least significant bit, tracking every carry, until the full sum including the final carry-out is known.

variants.label: Variant: a carry in every column

examples.title: Worked example: from a truth table to a sum of minterms
examples.objective: Turn a truth table into the canonical sum of minterms by writing one full product term for each row where the function is 1.

examples.title: Worked example: simplifying an expression law by law
examples.objective: Simplify a Boolean expression by applying one named algebra law at a time until no law can shrink it further, then confirm the equivalence on every truth-table row.

examples.title: Worked example: two dice, building the sample space
examples.objective: Construct the 36-pair sample space for two dice as a grid, mark an event on it, and compute the probability as a reduced fraction of the two counts.

examples.title: Worked example: conditional probability and an independence test
examples.objective: Compute a conditional probability by restricting the sample space to the given event, then test independence by comparing the exact fractions P(A and B) and P(A) times P(B).

variants.label: Variant: a pair that is independent

examples.title: Worked example: expected value, term by term
examples.objective: Build an expected value one term at a time from a payout table, keep a running total, and interpret the result as a fair price and a long-run average.

variants.label: Variant: the top prize drops to $3

examples.title: Worked example: Bayes with 1,000 dots
examples.objective: Use natural frequencies — counts out of 1,000 people — to find the probability that a positive test result is a true case, keeping the base rate in sight the whole way.

examples.title: Worked example: exactly 2 heads in 4 flips, by tree
examples.objective: Build the full outcome tree for repeated coin flips, collect the leaves with the target head count, and turn the leaf count into a probability.

examples.title: Worked example: designing the duplicate sign-up check
examples.objective: Run one real design problem through the whole loop — model, specification, cost analysis, then verification — and let the counting, not taste, choose the data structure.

examples.title: Worked example: designing a prerequisite-proof course schedule
examples.objective: Design a course schedule by modeling prerequisites as a directed acyclic graph, computing earliest semesters from the longest chain, verifying the plan mechanically against every prerequisite pair, and folding in a changed requirement.

examples.title: Worked example: designing an access rule and checking its form
examples.objective: Design a grant/deny rule as a Boolean formula, count its granting truth-table rows, verify a proposed form of the rule by exhaustive row-by-row comparison, and fold in an added condition.
